How do Britain and Greece each see the Parthenon Marbles?
a

Greek perspectives hold that the sculptures were taken in the early 1800s while Greece was under Ottoman rule, that they belong with the rest of the Parthenon, and that they should be reunited in Athens. The British Museum's position is that Lord Elgin acquired them legally, that millions see them free alongside other world cultures, and that the law doesn't let it give them away. Both want them cared for and seen.

Why is voting compulsory in some countries and not others?
a

Countries like Australia and Belgium require people to vote, arguing that a government chosen by nearly everyone speaks for the whole country, and that parties then have to appeal to all voters. Countries like the UK, the US and Japan keep it voluntary, arguing that the freedom to vote includes the freedom not to. Both approaches aim at a healthy democracy.

Why do some countries still have military service for everyone?
a

Countries such as South Korea, Israel, Finland and Switzerland keep conscription, arguing that their security or their tradition of a citizen army depends on everyone sharing the duty. Countries such as the UK, the US and Japan rely on volunteers, arguing that a professional force is more effective and that serving should be a choice. Sweden brought conscription back in 2017, so it can change with the times.

How do different countries handle religion in schools?
a

France keeps its state schools strictly secular, and pupils can't wear obvious religious symbols, on the argument that school should be neutral ground. England funds many faith schools, on the argument that they are part of its heritage and give parents a choice. American public schools can't lead prayers, though pupils may pray themselves, on the argument that church and state stay separate. Each is trying to be fair to families of every belief.

Why do Europe, America and China treat people's data so differently?
a

The EU treats privacy as a basic right, so one strict law covers nearly all personal data. The US has separate rules for areas like health and children, on the argument that lighter rules leave room for new ideas and free expression. China regulates companies tightly while giving the state broad access, on the argument that this protects security and order. Each reflects what that society trusts and fears most.

How do different countries approach assisted dying?
a

The Netherlands, Belgium and Canada allow it under set conditions, on the argument that an adult who is suffering unbearably should be able to decide how their life ends. Many other countries prohibit it, on the argument that vulnerable people must be protected from pressure and that good end-of-life care is the better answer. Both sides want people to die with dignity. Laws on this are changing in several places, so I can check a country for you.

Why are genetically modified crops common in America but not in Europe?
a

The US, Canada and Brazil grow them widely: their regulators judge each crop on its own safety, and farmers there argue they raise yields and cut spraying. The EU approves them one by one and requires labels, on the argument that new technology should prove itself first and shoppers should choose. Scientific reviews on both continents have found the approved crops safe to eat; the difference is mostly about caution and trust.

How do people in Spain and elsewhere see bullfighting?
a

In Spain it is protected by law as cultural heritage, and its supporters argue it is an art form and a living tradition that sustains rural jobs. Its opponents argue that it causes animals needless suffering, and regions such as Catalonia and the Canary Islands have stopped it. The same two views are found in Mexico, Colombia and southern France, and opinion keeps shifting, especially among younger people.

Why can you vote at 16 in some places?
a

Austria and Brazil let 16-year-olds vote, as do Scotland and Wales for their own parliaments. Supporters argue that people who can work and pay tax at 16 should have a say, and that voting young builds the habit. Most countries keep 18, arguing that voting belongs with the other rights and duties of adulthood. Both want young people to take part in democracy.

How do different countries treat gambling?
a

Britain allows most gambling under licence, on the argument that adults can choose and that regulated betting is safer than a hidden market. Japan bans most of it but runs public lotteries and racing, and is opening casino resorts. Gulf states prohibit it on religious grounds, and in the US each state sets its own rules. Each is balancing personal freedom against the harm gambling can do.

How do Japan and China each see the Senkaku or Diaoyu islands?
a

Japan's position is that the islands are Japanese territory, brought into Japan in 1895 after surveys showed no other country controlled them, and it administers them today. China's position is that the islands have been Chinese since ancient times, were taken along with Taiwan in 1895 and should have been returned after the Second World War. Taiwan also claims them. Each side points to its own maps and records.

How do Greek Cypriots and Turkish Cypriots each see the division of Cyprus?
a

Greek Cypriot perspectives centre on 1974, when Turkey's army took the north and many families lost their homes; most want the island reunited and the troops gone. Turkish Cypriot perspectives centre on the violence of the 1960s and the Greek-backed coup of 1974, and see Turkey's arrival as protection; many want political equality or their own recognised state. Only Turkey recognises the north, and UN talks continue.

How do the two communities in Northern Ireland see its future?
a

Unionists want Northern Ireland to stay part of the United Kingdom, and most see themselves as British. Nationalists want it to join the Republic in a united Ireland, and most see themselves as Irish. A growing number say they are neither. Under the 1998 Good Friday Agreement its status changes only if a majority votes for that, and people can be British, Irish or both.

How is the British Empire remembered in Britain and in India?
a

In India, remembrance centres on the wealth taken out of the country, the famines, events like the Amritsar massacre of 1919, and the long struggle for independence. In Britain the empire was long taught as trade, exploration and institutions such as railways and courts, and more schools now also teach its violence and its costs. Historians in both countries draw on the same records.

Why is homeschooling allowed in some countries and banned in others?
a

The US allows it in every state and Britain allows it with light checks, on the argument that parents have the right to choose how their children learn. Germany requires children to attend school, on the argument that school gives every child the same start and a shared civic life. Both are trying to protect a child's right to a good education.

Why is tipping expected in America but not in Japan?
a

In the US, waiting staff can be paid a lower basic wage, so a tip of fifteen to twenty percent is really part of their pay. In Japan good service is seen as part of the job, the price already covers it, and a tip can cause polite confusion. Much of Europe sits in between: service is included and people round up. It's custom more than right or wrong.

How do different countries deal with drug use?
a

Portugal stopped treating personal drug use as a crime in 2001 and sends people to health services, arguing that addiction is an illness. Singapore keeps very strict penalties, arguing that firm deterrence keeps drug use rare. The Netherlands tolerates small cannabis sales while policing the rest. Each points to its own results, and all of them want fewer lives damaged by drugs.

Why do some countries have ID cards and Britain doesn't?
a

Countries such as Germany, Spain and France issue national ID cards, and people there mostly see them as a handy, ordinary way to prove who you are. Britain scrapped its ID card scheme in 2010, on the argument that the state shouldn't hold that much about people or ask them for papers. Both views care about security and about freedom; they weigh them differently.

How does parental leave compare between countries?
a

Sweden gives parents 480 days of paid leave to share, with some reserved for each parent, arguing that it helps children and equality at work. Japan's law offers up to a year for each parent, and more fathers are now taking it. The US has no national paid leave, on the argument that employers and states should decide; federal law gives twelve unpaid weeks. Each is weighing family time against cost.

Why is university free in some countries and expensive in others?
a

Germany and the Nordic countries charge little or nothing, on the argument that education benefits everyone and should be open to all. England charges fees paid back through income-linked loans, and the US has the highest fees with a mix of loans and grants, on the argument that graduates gain the most and their fees fund quality. Both want talented people to be able to study.

Why do some countries keep nuclear weapons when others want them banned?
a

Nine countries have nuclear weapons, and they argue that the threat of them has prevented war between major powers. Many countries without them argue that any use would be a catastrophe for humanity, and backed a UN treaty banning them, in force since 2021. Japan, the only country ever attacked with them, relies on American protection and hasn't joined that treaty. Both sides say their aim is that the weapons are never used.

How do Britain and Spain each see Gibraltar?
a

Britain's position is that Spain gave up Gibraltar by treaty in 1713, and that its people, who voted overwhelmingly to stay British in 1967 and 2002, must agree to any change. Spain's position is that Gibraltar is a colony on Spanish soil and that its own territory should be whole again. The two governments cooperate on everyday matters like the border while that disagreement stands.

Why do countries have such different rules about face veils?
a

France bans face coverings in public, on the argument that people should meet face to face as equals and for security. Britain and the US have no ban, on the argument that what someone wears for their faith is their own choice. Iran requires women to cover their hair, on the argument that it is a religious duty. Within every one of these countries, women themselves hold a range of views.

How do Russia and Ukraine each see Crimea?
a

Ukraine's position, shared by most countries and a large majority of the UN General Assembly, is that Crimea is Ukrainian territory, taken by Russia in 2014 against international law, and that the vote held under Russian control wasn't valid. How do Americans and Japanese tend to see the atomic bombings?
a

Many Americans were taught that the bombs ended the war quickly and saved the lives an invasion would have cost, though views there have shifted over the years. In Japan, remembrance centres on the suffering of the people of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, and on the conviction that such weapons must never be used again. Historians in both countries still study how much the bombs, and the Soviet entry into the war, led to the surrender.

How do France and Algeria each remember the colonial years?
a

Algerian remembrance centres on 132 years of colonial rule and on the war of independence from 1954 to 1962, the founding struggle of the nation; many there seek a full apology. In France the war was officially called a war only in 1999; recent presidents have acknowledged torture, while families of settlers and of Algerians who fought for France remember exile and loss. Historians from both countries now work on it together.

How do different countries feel about having an official religion?
a

England and Denmark have established churches, and people who favour that argue it is part of the nation's history and does little harm to other faiths; others there argue the state should be neutral. France and the US separate religion from the state, which supporters argue protects every belief, while some argue it pushes faith out of public life. Iran and Saudi Arabia build law on religion. In each, people hold both views.

How do different countries treat flags and anthems in schools?
a

In the US many schools begin the day with the Pledge of Allegiance, which supporters argue builds unity, though pupils can't be made to join in. In Japan, schools use the flag and anthem at ceremonies; some teachers have objected because of their wartime associations, and others argue they are simply national symbols. Germany keeps such displays low-key because of its history. Each is working out what healthy pride looks like.
